title: Redwood demo - Structured Output & Function Calling (JSON mode)
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Atlas Health through Console and API demos focused on structured output (JSON mode), schema enforcement, and function/tool calling. Customer probed latency/cost tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted, SOC2/KMS, and request a POC + security docs. Agreed next steps: send pricing/sku, security pack, schedule POC baseline benchmark and follow-up with SE to scope metrics.
topics: Deployment options: hosted vs dedicated vs private
action_items: Samira: Send pricing sheet and dedicated capacity SKUs by 2026-05-14
Diego: Share POC runbook + benchmarking spreadsheet (latency/cost template) by 2026-05-15
Samira: Attach SOC 2 and security pack + KMS integration notes to the thread by 2026-05-14
Jordan: Provide sample prompt set and 3 representative API workloads by 2026-05-18
next_steps: Schedule 2-week POC: Redwood to provision sandbox Dedicated trial (or hosted POC) to run 1k requests/day baseline
SE to run latency/cost baseline and share results in shared sheet
Follow-up call w/ Atlas Security to review KMS and VPC requirements
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. I'm Samira with Redwood, AE for this account. With me are Diego and Lena from solutions. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Maya: Good, thanks. Excited to see the structured output stuff — we want deterministic JSON for downstream systems.
[00:12] Diego: Awesome. Today we'll show JSON mode, schemas and the function-calling flow, plus how Console surfaces guardrails and Optimize suggestions. We'll demo both the API and Console.
[00:22] Priya: Quick note — our main concern is any hallucinated keys breaking our ingestion pipeline, and also latency under our 300ms p95 requirement.
[00:30] Diego: Totally. We'll show schema validation and a fail-safe path (like a validation error) and also how to route to a simpler model fallback.
[00:40] Evan: From security side — SOC 2, KMS support, audit logs, and VPC options matter.
[00:46] Samira: Yep we'll cover those; we'll also attach the security pack after.
[00:52] [01:03] Diego: I'm switching to the Console now — bear with me while the deck loads. You can see the API keys area, model catalog, and on the right the structured output toggle.
[01:20] Diego: (screen) Here is a JSON schema we declared — you can define types, required fields, enums. I'll paste an example: order_id string, total_amount number, items array with object schema, customer.email format string. Also you can mark fields as nullable.
[01:40] Jordan: Is that the same schema format as OpenAPI or a simplified JSON Schema?
[01:45] Diego: It's standard JSON Schema-ish; we support common validators but keep it friendly. The runtime will return a validation result with error codes.
[01:55] Diego: Now I'll run a sample prompt: "Extract order data from this invoice text" and set mode=json, temperature=0, max_tokens=300.
[02:12] [02:20] (typing)
[02:28] Diego: Response comes back — you can see validated=true and the structured payload. If a required key is missing the SDK response includes validation.errors and we can set a strict mode to throw an API error rather than returning partial output.
[02:45] Maya: Can you show function or tool calling after that? We want to trigger downstream services only when payload passes checks.
[02:52] Diego: Sure. There's a function-calling extension — you register a function signature, name, and Redwood can produce a function call object instead of free text. In the Console demo I'll show 'create_invoice' function with args matching the schema.
[03:06] (clicks)
[03:12] Diego: Sending same prompt but with function calling enabled... response is a call to create_invoice with args JSON that match the schema. The Console also highlights discrepancies like types mismatched.
[03:30] Jordan: What happens if the model hallucinates a field value with wrong type? Is there automatic coercion?
[03:36] Diego: Good Q. You can toggle coercion. By default Redwood will not coerce — it'll flag and either return an error or send an explainable validation object. You can also enable a lightweight transformation layer to try coercions (e.g., "123" -> number) but we log that and tag it in the audit trail.
[03:56] Priya: How about guardrails for enumerations — e.g., status must be [PENDING, PAID, REFUNDED]?
[04:02] Diego: We support enums; if the output is outside enum we mark validation.failed and optionally trigger a fallback model or human-in-the-loop.
[04:18] [04:25] Samira: For production we've seen customers use a two-step pipeline: structured extraction + validator -> if fails then reroute to lower-latency cached model or human review. That keeps throughput high.
[04:35] Maya: Can we set up canary rollouts for a model change?
[04:39] Lena: Yes, Redwood Console has rollout controls — you can do percentage-based canaries, A/B traffic splits across model variants, and instant rollback on regression detection tied to evaluation sets.
[04:52] Evan: On dedicated vs hosted — we need predictable tail latency. Is dedicated the right move?
[04:58] Samira: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity and guaranteed throughput; hosted is faster to start but tail latencies can vary depending on multi-tenant load. Dedicated also comes with SLA options.
[05:12] Jordan: Cost delta?
[05:15] Samira: We'll send a SKU sheet but rough rule: dedicated is higher fixed commit but lower unit cost at scale and more predictable p95. Hosted is pay-as-you-go, easier operationally.
[05:28] [05:35] Diego: Back to the demo — I'm going to show API snippet. The SDK call includes model, mode: 'json', schema: { ... }, functions: [{name: 'create_invoice', args_schema: {...}}], and call options like max_tokens, stop, temperature.
[05:55] Diego: For function calling we return a 'function_call' object with name + args serialized. Your app is responsible for executing the function; Redwood can be configured to auto-invoke via connectors if you wire a webhook.
[06:12] Priya: Do you have built-in connectors for common sinks, or is it custom?
[06:16] Diego: We have connectors for common storage (S3), message buses, and you can plug in webhooks. For fully managed invocation we offer secure connectors with VPC peering for private deployments.
[06:29] Maya: How do you handle secrets when invoking external functions? KMS?
[06:33] Diego: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS for Private deployments and dedicated, plus secret stores and token redaction in logs. Audit logs capture invocation metadata but not raw secrets.
[06:45] Evan: We need proof — can you share SOC2 cert and architecture notes?
[06:49] Samira: Yes, action item — we'll attach SOC2, penetration test summary, and KMS integration docs after the call.
[06:56] [07:02] Diego: Switching to the Optimize tab — this is where Redwood suggests batching and quantization settings per workload. It analyzes token distribution and suggests a quantization profile (e.g., q4_0 or q8_0) and ideal batch size to hit p95 SLA while minimizing cost.
[07:20] Diego: For highly structured extraction workloads we often recommend temperature=0, small max tokens, and using KV prefix caching where possible to reduce repeated encoder work. That lowers cost per token.
[07:34] Jordan: Do Optimize suggestions run automatically or are they prescriptive?
[07:38] Lena: They're recommendations, you can apply them as a policy to a route — for Dedicated you can enforce policies across a pool. We also show simulated cost impacts so you can preview savings.
[07:50] Priya: Any example numbers?
[07:52] Diego: Example: moving from float16 to q4_0 and enabling batching saved one customer ~30% unit cost with negligible p95 change for extraction workloads. YMMV of course.
[08:04] [08:10] Maya: Latency numbers — if we have 300ms p95 target, can you run a baseline against our sample workload?
[08:16] Diego: Yes, that's part of the POC. We'll run a bench with your prompt set and measure p50/p95/p99, tokens per request, and cost per 1k requests. We'll propose batching and a model variant to meet your budget/SLO.
[08:29] Samira: We'll include a cost/latency tradeoff chart in the POC deliverable.
[08:33] Jordan: For schema enforcement, is the validation synchronous? I.e., is validation computed before returning the response?
[08:39] Diego: Validation is synchronous in the response path — the runtime runs a lightweight validator against the output. That adds minimal overhead (milliseconds) but we surface validation metadata. If strict_mode is on we return 4xx errors for validation failures.
[08:54] Evan: Are validation logs stored? For compliance we need long-term retention for 12 months.
[08:59] Samira: Audit logs, including validation outcomes and function invocation metadata, can be exported to your logging bucket; retention configurable with enterprise plans.
[09:10] [09:15] Priya: About model updates — how do we lock a version so the output doesn't change unexpectedly?
[09:20] Lena: You can pin model versions or pin a model tag in Redwood. We also support automatic evaluation against your prompt set on model updates and can block rollouts for regressions.
[09:34] Maya: Can the Console show diffs between two model outputs on a test set?
[09:38] Diego: Yes — evaluation run will show per-case diffs, quality metrics, and a regression heatmap.
[09:46] [09:55] Samira: Quick reprioritization — Jordan, for the POC we'll need your sample prompts and a few target SLOs, and Evan from security we'll set a separate call just for KMS/VPC specifics.
[10:06] Jordan: Sounds good. We'll collate 1000 sample requests and tag the ones that must be 300ms p95.
[10:13] Evan: I'll pull network diagrams and our KMS policy.
[10:17] [10:25] Priya: One last technical question — if function calling returns args but the downstream service times out, do you have retry semantics or idempotency helpers?
[10:33] Diego: We expose invocation metadata with request IDs and idempotency keys. Retries are recommended to be handled by the application layer; Redis-based idempotency helpers are common. Redwood connectors can perform managed retries with exponential backoff.
[10:46] Maya: Also curious about small-batch latency — if we force batch size >1 for efficiency, will that hurt p95?
[10:53] Diego: It depends. Batching increases throughput but adds queueing latency. Optimize will recommend batch sizes based on your latency distribution, and you can use dynamic batching thresholds to maintain p95 SLO.
[11:06] [11:12] Samira: We'll include a recommended batch policy in the POC deliverable.
[11:16] (brief pause)
[11:22] Diego: Now I'll show a failed-validation flow: I'll purposely remove an 'items' field in the output and show strict_mode on — API returns 422 with validation.errors and error codes. Console highlights the failing request and you can replay it.
[11:40] Jordan: Nice — replay is useful for debugging. Does replay include the KV cache state?
[11:44] Diego: We snapshot relevant metadata including recent KV cache keys for deterministic reproductions where possible — we call it request context tracing. Sometimes cache is ephemeral but we capture enough to reproduce.
[11:56] Evan: For Private deployments, is the control plane still Redwood-hosted or customer-hosted?
[12:01] Lena: Control plane can be customer-hosted for fully air-gapped/regulated environments; we offer an on-prem package. If control plane is customer-hosted, logs and keys stay in your environment.
[12:14] Maya: Any additional compliance docs beyond SOC2? We may need ISO and penetration test reports.
[12:19] Samira: We'll surface what we have; ISO in progress last I heard, but pen test summary is available.
[12:25] [12:30] Priya: Can we set up RBAC so only product team can kick off model rollouts?
[12:35] Lena: Yes RBAC + SSO + audit trails. You can bind roles to routes and require approvals for rollouts.
[12:44] Jordan: Pricing question — for function-calling flows where we only store small payloads, how are we billed? Token-based? Invocation-based?
[12:51] Samira: Billing is token-based for inference plus optional invocation/unit fees for connectors in managed mode; we'll clarify in the SKU sheet.
[12:59] [13:05] Diego: Wrapping up the demo — Console also has a test harness where you can run a suite of prompts and assert expected JSON keys; failing cases are grouped. This is how we automate regression checks during rollouts.
[13:20] Maya: That test harness will help our QA sign-off.
[13:24] Evan: Security-only call next week?
[13:27] Samira: Yes we'll schedule a separate security deep-dive — Evan, can you share calendar availability?
[13:31] Evan: I'll send times.
[13:34] [13:40] Priya: For timelines — if POC goes well, we're aiming for pilot in Q3 with a production rollout by end of Q3.
[13:46] Samira: Good. We'll treat that as target.
[13:50] Jordan: One more thing — can we do an end-to-end demo where create_invoice actually writes to our sandbox S3 and we validate ingestion?
[13:58] Diego: Absolutely — Redwood connector to S3 can write to your sandbox bucket; we'll coordinate IAM role.
[14:06] [14:10] Samira: Recap of next steps: send pricing and security pack, SE to share POC runbook and benchmarking sheet, Atlas to provide sample prompts and SLOs, schedule security deep-dive.
[14:22] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[14:25] Samira: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with links.
[14:30] (call ends)

Notes: transcription includes occasional mislabels and small OCR-like errors (e.g., K-V cash, Red-word) in the transcript; punctuation and speaker tags follow typical Fireflies export style. References: demo deck link: https://redwood.example.com/decks/structured-output, security pack link: https://redwood.example.com/security/pack.zip, benchmark sheet link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/atlas-baseline.xlsx
